fatal_errors: The proposed Ti/Ni coating does not reconstruct the target intervention: liquid-metal dealloying of a directionally segregated WTaVTi precursor in molten Cu at 1200 °C for 96 h.
The hypothesis omits the target bicontinuous, directionally aligned RHEA-ligament/Cu-channel architecture and the spontaneously formed W-rich interlayer.
The cited evidence concerns Ti/Ni-coated diamond particles in a high-entropy-alloy matrix, not W–Cu interfaces, thermal conductivity, or irradiation resistance.
No evidence supports retention of irradiation resistance by a Ti/Ni interlayer under fusion-relevant exposure.
Application conditions and irradiation dose, species, energy, temperature, and fluence are not operationally defined.
explanation: The response addresses the broad W–Cu design goal and proposes a controlled comparison against an uncoated composite, but it is not an evidence-supported reconstruction of the target study. The target used liquid-metal dealloying to selectively replace Ti/V-rich interdendritic channels in WTaVTi with Cu, creating aligned conductive channels, continuous refractory-HEA ligaments, and a W-rich passivating interface. The generated mechanism instead invokes a deliberately deposited Ti/Ni coating on conventional W particles. Its supporting paper only demonstrates improved bonding and mechanical properties for coated diamond/HEA composites and provides no direct basis for enhanced W–Cu thermal transport or irradiation stability. The proposed experiment could test the alternative in principle, but it needs quantitative conditions and separate non-inferiority thresholds for durability and irradiation resistance; its current falsification rule is also logically ambiguous because failure in any one required property should falsify the combined claim.
